A personal account of manuscripts kept by a lawyer illustrates the interest in proving when work existed, without establishing what legal protection those methods provide.

evidence.note: Describes teaching about engineers who failed commercially and discusses patents, records of conception and personal manuscript storage.

segments.summary: The engineering-teaching digression separates technical achievement from the commercial work needed to retain control of it.

segments.title: Where could England accommodate a new large shipyard?
segments.body: A large new yard needs enough flat coastal land for slipways, dry docks, cranes and covered working areas. An established industrial setting is preferred because shipbuilding is more likely to be acceptable locally. The proposal assumes that facilities would be built in concrete, allowing a large flat site to be adapted to the yard's requirements. Dungeness is considered for its terrain, with the bird observatory and surrounding uses complicating the choice. Expanding Cammell Laird on the Mersey is the instinctive preference because a functioning yard already exists, but development around it limits room. Middlesbrough raises similar concerns, while industrial land nearer the mouth of the Tees is another possibility. Areas around Felixstowe and the Orwell are also considered, with farmland among the competing uses. A later reply dismisses much of Cornwall as too hilly and notes pressure on space at Falmouth. These are tentative comparisons of constraints, with no fully assessed site selected.

evidence.note: Considers space requirements and local acceptance of industry, gives Cammell Laird as the instinctive preference while noting surrounding development, and compares Dungeness, the Mersey, Middlesbrough, the Tees and the Orwell area.
Adds Cornwall's hilly terrain and Falmouth's constrained space to the comparison.

segments.summary: A large shipyard needs flat coastal land and room to expand, with housing, existing industry and other land uses constraining the options.
segments.question: Where would you put a new large shipyard if it had to be in England?
segments.answerShort: The instinctive preference is to expand Cammell Laird, although surrounding development is a major obstacle. A new site would need ample flat coastal land; Dungeness, the Tees and the Orwell are considered without a final choice.

segments.title: Was Churchill the best available mentor for Elizabeth II?
segments.body: Churchill is judged the best available option for the role described in the question. The answer allows that one could imagine a better mentor in the abstract. Attlee is treated as a capable alternative in personal terms, but he lacked the parliamentary majority required to occupy the office. The judgment therefore depends on the choices available at the time.

evidence.note: Assesses Churchill against politically available alternatives and notes Attlee's lack of a majority.

segments.summary: The answer distinguishes an ideal mentor from a person who was politically available to serve as prime minister.
segments.question: Was Churchill the best available prime minister to mentor Elizabeth II because of his sense of duty?
segments.answerShort: The answer judges him the best available option, while acknowledging Attlee's qualities and the political constraint of his lacking a majority.

segments.title: Which later admirals merit warship names?
segments.body: The question requests ten admirals who served after 1850 as names for a major warship class. Clearly stated choices include Cunningham, Henderson, Sherbrooke, Forbes, Fraser, Fisher, Jellicoe and Beatty. Beatty receives a reluctant acknowledgment that he merits the honour. A further proposed name is unclear, and the exchange does not establish a complete ten-name list. The rank criterion excludes a suggested commodore. A later suggestion of Scott is rejected on the grounds that research ships already bear his name, although the reply does not identify him further.

evidence.note: Lists eight clearly identifiable choices, includes one unclear additional name and rejects a commodore under the question's rank criterion.
Declines the suggestion of Scott because research ships already carry his name, without identifying him further.

segments.summary: The naming exercise produces several clear choices, including a reluctant acknowledgment of Beatty.
segments.question: Which admirals who served after 1850 would you use as names for a ten-ship class?
segments.answerShort: The clear choices are Cunningham, Henderson, Sherbrooke, Forbes, Fraser, Fisher, Jellicoe and Beatty; the answer does not establish all ten names.

segments.title: Will another submarine be named Churchill?
segments.body: Another nuclear-powered attack submarine named Churchill is considered unlikely. No further reason or confirmed naming plan is offered.

evidence.note: Briefly answers the question with a doubtful prediction.

segments.summary: Another Royal Navy SSN named Churchill is considered unlikely.
segments.question: Will another SSN be named after Churchill?
segments.answerShort: Another SSN named Churchill is considered unlikely; this is a prediction, not a confirmed naming decision.

segments.title: Warship names and diplomatic offence
segments.body: Land victories over present allies, including the United States and France, are offered as the most provocative naming principle. Six individual battle names are not supplied. The suggestion is explicitly treated as something Britain would not do, illustrating the diplomatic sensitivity of public commemoration.

evidence.note: Answers with the principle of commemorating land victories over current allies, without supplying six specific names.

segments.summary: A humorous naming question illustrates why commemorating victories over present allies can be awkward.
segments.question: What names for a six-ship class would cause Britain the most diplomatic trouble?
segments.answerShort: The suggestion is victories over present allies, although no six-name list is supplied and the idea is treated as deliberately provocative.
